entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 2 Ha 2:1-20 . The Prophet, Waiting Earnestly for an Answer to His Complaints (First Chapter), Receives a Revelation, Which Is to Be Fulfilled, Not Immediately, Yet in Due Time, and Is Therefore to Be Waited for in Faith: The Chaldeans Shall Be Punished for Their Cruel Rapacity, nor Can Their False GodS Avert the Judgment of Jehovah, the Only True God. 1. stand upon ... watch-- that is, watch-post. The prophets often compare themselves, awaiting the revelations of Jehovah with earnest patience, to watchmen on an eminence watching with intent eye all that comes within their view ( Is 21:8 , 11 ; Jr 6:17 ; Eze 3:17 ; 33:2 , 3 ; compare Psa 5:3 ; 85:8 ). The "watch-post" is the withdrawal of the whole soul from earthly, and fixing it on heavenly, things. The accumulation of synonyms, "stand upon ... watch ... set me upon ... tower ... watch to see" implies persevering fixity of attention. what he will say unto me-- in answer to my complaints ( Ha 1:13 ). Literally, "in me," God speaking, not to the prophet's outward ear, but inwardly. When we have prayed to God, we must observe what answers God gives by His word, His Spirit, and His providences. what I shall answer when I am reproved-- what answer I am to make to the reproof which I anticipate from God on account of the liberty of my expostulation with Him. Maurer translates, "What I am to answer in respect to my complaint against Jehovah" ( Ha 1:12-17 ).

Write the vision--</hi>which I am about to reveal to thee.<div eID="gen24042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make it plain--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.27.8">De 27:8</reference>). In large legible characters.<div eID="gen24043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon tables--</hi>boxwood tables covered with wax, on which national affairs were engraved with an iron pen, and then hung up in public, at the prophets' own houses, or at the temple, that those who passed might read them. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.63">Lu 1:63</reference>, "writing table," that is, tablet.<div eID="gen24044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may run that readeth it--</hi>commonly explained, "so intelligible as to be easily read by any one running past"; but then it would be, "that he that runneth may read it." The true sense is, "so legible that whoever readeth it, may run to tell all whom he can the good news of the foe's coming doom, and Judah's deliverance." Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Da 12:4</reference>, "many shall run to and fro," namely, with the explanation of the prophecy, then unsealed; also, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>, "let him that heareth (the good news) say (to every one within his reach), Come." "Run" is equivalent to announce the divine revelation (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jr 23:21</reference>); as everyone who becomes informed of a divine message is bound to run, that is, use all despatch to make it known to others [Henderson]. Grotius, Ludovicus De Dieu, and Maurer interpret it: "Run" is not literal running, but "that he who reads it may run through it," that is, read it at once without difficulty. <div eID="gen24045" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12886"/><div sID="gen24050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12886"/><hi type="bold">4. his soul which is lifted up--</hi>the Chaldean's [Maurer]. The unbelieving Jew's [Henderson].<div eID="gen24050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is not upright in him--</hi>that is, is not accounted upright in God's sight; in antithesis to "shall live." So <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>, which with inspired authority applies the general sense to the particular case which Paul had in view, "If any man draw back (one result of being 'lifted up' with overweening arrogancy), my soul shall have no pleasure in him."<div eID="gen24051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the just shall live by his faith--</hi>the Jewish nation, as opposed to the unbelieving Chaldean (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>) [Maurer]. Henderson's view is that the believing Jew is meant, as opposed to the unbelieving Jew (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">Ga 3:11</reference>). The believing Jew, though God's promise tarry, will wait for it; the unbelieving "draws back," as <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference> expresses it. The sense, in Maurer's view, which accords better with the context (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>, &c.). is: the Chaldean, though for a time seeming to prosper, yet being lifted up with haughty unbelief (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Ha 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>), is not upright; that is, has no right stability of soul resting on God, to ensure permanence of prosperity; hence, though for a time executing God's judgments, he at last becomes "lifted up" so as to attribute to his own power what is the work of God, and in this sense "draws back" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>), becoming thereby a type of all backsliders who thereby incur God's displeasure; as the believing Jew is of all who wait for God's promises with patient faith, and so "live" (stand accepted) before God. The Hebrew accents induce Bengel to translate, "he who is just by his faith shall live." Other manuscripts read the accents as English Version, which agrees better with Hebrew syntax. <div eID="gen24052" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12887"/><div sID="gen24053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12887"/><hi type="bold">5. Yea also, because--</hi>additional reason why the Jews may look for God punishing their Chaldean foe, namely, because ... he is<div eID="gen24053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a proud man--</hi>rather, this clause continues the reason for the Jews expecting the punishment of the Chaldeans, "because he transgresseth by wine (a besetting sin of Babylon, compare <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>, and Curtius [5.1]), being a proud man." Love of wine often begets a proud contempt of divine things, as in Belshazzar's case, which was the immediate cause of the fall of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.2-Dan.4.30">Da 5:2-4, 30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.20.1">Pr 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">31:5</reference>).<div eID="gen24054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enlargeth his desire as hell--</hi>the grave, or the unseen world, which is "never full" (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pr 27:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.16">30:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Is 5:14</reference>). The Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar were filled with an insatiable desire of conquest. Another reason for their punishment. <div eID="gen24055" type="x-p"/>

Shall not all these--</hi>the "nations" and "peoples" (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>) "heaped unto him" by the Chaldean.<div eID="gen24056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take up a parable--</hi>a derisive song. Habakkuk follows Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>) and Micah (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>) in the phraseology.<div eID="gen24057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against him--</hi>when dislodged from his former eminence.<div eID="gen24058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Woe--</hi>The "derisive song" here begins, and continues to the end of the chapter. It is a symmetrical whole, and consists of five stanzas, the first three consisting of three verses each, the fourth of four verses, and the last of two. Each stanza has its own subject, and all except the last begin with "Woe"; and all have a closing verse introduced with "for," "because," or "but."<div eID="gen24059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how long?--</hi>how long destined to retain his ill-gotten gains? But for a short time, as his fall now proves [Maurer]. "Covetousness is the greatest bane to men. For they who invade others' goods, often lose even their own" [Menander]. Calvin makes "how long?" to be the cry of those groaning under the Chaldean oppression while it still lasted: How long shall such oppression be permitted to continue? But it is plainly part of the derisive song, after the Chaldean tyranny had passed away.<div eID="gen24060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ladeth himself with thick clay--</hi>namely, gold and silver dug out of the "clay," of which they are a part. The covetous man in heaping them together is only lading himself with a clay burden, as he dares not enjoy them, and is always anxious about them. Lee and Fuller translate the Hebrew as a reduplicated single noun, and not two words, "an accumulation of pledges" (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.10-Deut.24.13">De 24:10-13</reference>). The Chaldean is compared to a harsh usurer, and his ill-gotten treasures to heaps of pledges in the hands of a usurer. <div eID="gen24061" type="x-p"/>

It is a symmetrical whole, and consists of five stanzas, the first three consisting of three verses each, the fourth of four verses, and the last of two. Calvin makes "how long?" to be the cry of those groaning under the Chaldean oppression while it still lasted: How long shall such oppression be permitted to continue? But it is plainly part of the derisive song, after the Chaldean tyranny had passed away. ladeth himself with thick clay-- namely, gold and silver dug out of the "clay," of which they are a part. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12897"/><div sID="gen24079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12897"/><hi type="bold">15. giveth ... neighbour drink ... puttest ... bottle to him--</hi>literally, "skin," as the Easterns use "bottles" of skin for wine. Maurer, from a different Hebrew root, translates, "that pourest in thy wrath." English Version keeps up the metaphor better. It is not enough for thee to be "drunken" thyself, unless thou canst lead others into the same state. The thing meant is, that the Chaldean king, with his insatiable desires (a kind of intoxication), allured neighboring states into the same mad thirst for war to obtain booty, and then at last exposed them to loss and shame (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>; Ob 16). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12899"/><div sID="gen24087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12899"/><hi type="bold">17. the violence of Lebanon--</hi>thy "violence" against "Lebanon," that is, Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Is 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">Jr 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12">12</reference>; for Lebanon's cedars were used in building the temple and houses of Jerusalem; and its beauty made it a fit type of the metropolis), shall fall on thine own head.<div eID="gen24087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cover--</hi>that is, completely overwhelm.<div eID="gen24088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid--</hi>Maurer explains, "the spoiling inflicted on the beasts of Lebanon (that is, on the people of Jerusalem, of which city 'Lebanon' is the type), which made them afraid (shall cover thee)." But it seems inappropriate to compare the elect people to "beasts." I therefore prefer explaining, "the spoiling of beasts," that is, such as is inflicted on beasts caught in a net, and "which makes them afraid (shall cover thee)." Thus the Babylonians are compared to wild beasts terrified at being caught suddenly in a net. In cruel rapacity they resembled wild beasts. The ancients read, "the spoiling of wild beasts shall make THEE afraid." Or else explain, "the spoiling of beasts (the Medes and Persians) which (inflicted by thee) made them afraid (shall in turn cover thyself--revert on thyself from them)." This accords better with the parallel clause, "the violence of Lebanon," that is, inflicted by thee on Lebanon. As thou didst hunt men as wild beasts, so shalt thou be hunted thyself as a wild beast, which thou resemblest in cruelty.<div eID="gen24089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of men's blood--</hi>shed by thee; repeated from <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>. The ancients read, "the spoiling of wild beasts shall make THEE afraid." Or else explain, "the spoiling of beasts (the Medes and Persians) which (inflicted by thee) made them afraid (shall in turn cover thyself--revert on thyself from them)." This accords better with the parallel clause, "the violence of Lebanon," that is, inflicted by thee on Lebanon. As thou didst hunt men as wild beasts, so shalt thou be hunted thyself as a wild beast, which thou resemblest in cruelty. because of men's blood-- shed by thee; repeated from Ha 2:8 . But here the "land" and "city" are used of Judea and Jerusalem: not of the earth and cities generally, as in Ha 2:8 . the violence of the land, &c.-- that is, inflicted on the land by thee.
